title: Child-care difficulty converts time and money into unequal work adaptations
source_unit: U.S. Census Bureau 2025 CPS ASEC working paper; households with children ages 0–13, reference year 2024

observations.period: 2024 reference year; 2025 CPS ASEC collection and May 2026 Census working paper

denominator.unit: US households reporting a child age 0–13; 7.3 million used paid care

mean_paid_childcare_spending.unit: US dollars among households with nonzero paid-care spending

mean_childcare_income_share.unit: percent of household income among households with paid-care spending

adequate_care_problem.unit: percent of households with children reporting problems obtaining care that prevented more work

mean_work_days_lost.unit: converted work days among households reporting a child-care problem

below_100_fpl_work_days_lost.unit: converted work days among affected households below 100% FPL

paid_leave_adaptation.unit: percent of households with children selecting paid leave; adaptations are not mutually exclusive

unpaid_leave_adaptation.unit: percent of households with children selecting unpaid leave; adaptations are not mutually exclusive

cut_hours_adaptation.unit: percent of households with children selecting reduced work hours; adaptations are not mutually exclusive

quit_job_adaptation.unit: percent of households with children selecting job quitting; adaptations are not mutually exclusive

did_not_look_for_job_adaptation.unit: percent of households with children selecting non-search; adaptations are not mutually exclusive

supervised_while_working_adaptation.unit: percent of households with children selecting supervision while working; adaptations are not mutually exclusive

low_income_paid_leave.unit: percent below 100% FPL selecting paid leave

high_income_paid_leave.unit: percent above 400% FPL selecting paid leave

low_income_nonsearch.unit: percent below 100% FPL selecting did not look for a job

high_income_nonsearch.unit: percent above 400% FPL selecting did not look for a job

observations.method: Census analysis of new 2025 CPS ASEC child-care challenge and adaptation questions plus established expense, income, family, and labor-force measures; estimates use replicate weights and adaptations allow multiple responses.
observations.uncertainty: The reference period is 2024 and the paper is descriptive. Child-care problems, work-time loss, paid care, and adaptation categories have distinct universes; time lost is converted from hours/days/weeks with top-coding, and the paper does not follow households longitudinally or estimate a policy effect.
observations.subgroup: Households with children ages 0–13, conditioned by youngest-child age, poverty status, family structure, and reference-person/second-adult labor-force status.
observations.counterinterpretation: Lower-income households report less paid-care use and paid leave but more non-search, which may reflect limited access, different care arrangements, job conditions, or interpretation of the work-time question rather than lower care need; paid-care spending is not the total burden.

related_sources.claim: Official Census landing page gives paper title, date, authors, abstract, and PDF route.
Local memo preserves the care-to-work interpretation and open-arrow boundary.

boundary: This record establishes a descriptive household care-to-work adaptation surface for the 2024 reference year. It does not establish a dated provider disruption, subsidy or leave eligibility, causal child-care policy effect, wage/job loss, child outcome, later recovery, trust, political action, or longitudinal household trajectory.

reproduction_audit.retrieval_hash_scope: Official Census working-paper PDF retrieved and hashed; no CPS microdata downloaded
